reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: A venous malformation variant defined by the presence of glomus cells in the walls of the malformed venous channels
Caused by inherited loss-of-function variants in the glomulin (GLMN) gene, typically autosomal dominant with variable expression
Lesions are often multiple, bluish-to-purple, raised and cobblestoned, and frequently located on the extremities
In contrast to common venous malformations they are usually firmer, more nodular, less compressible and often painful or tender to focal pressure
A positive family history and multifocal cutaneous lesions favour the diagnosis over sporadic venous malformation
Because they are less compressible and more superficial, they respond less predictably to sclerotherapy than ordinary venous malformations
Histology demonstrates rows of glomus cells lining ectatic venous channels
Management is guided by symptoms and includes surgical excision for localised painful lesions and sclerotherapy or laser for selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Glomuvenous malformation is a slow-flow venous malformation distinguished by abnormal glomus cells, which are modified smooth-muscle cells, within the walls of dilated venous channels. It arises from loss-of-function variants in the glomulin (GLMN) gene inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, with a somatic second hit thought to determine where individual lesions develop. The glomus cells confer the characteristic firmness, nodularity, reduced compressibility and tenderness that separate these lesions from common venous malformations, and their differing structure explains their less predictable response to sclerotherapy.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination assessing compressibility, tenderness and multifocality
Doppler ultrasound to confirm slow-flow venous characteristics
MRI to define extent when lesions are large or deep
Histopathology demonstrating glomus cells around venous channels
Family history review and examination of relatives
redFlags: Severe or disabling pain from a lesion
Rapid enlargement or change in an established lesion
Functional impairment when lesions overlie joints or pressure areas
Diagnostic uncertainty raising concern for another vascular or soft-tissue lesion
reference.prognosis: Glomuvenous malformations are benign and do not undergo malignant change; they tend to persist and new lesions may appear over time, but symptoms are usually manageable, and localised painful lesions often do well with excision though multifocal disease can recur.
pitfalls: Managing them as ordinary venous malformations and expecting a good sclerotherapy response
Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and not exploring family history
Misdiagnosing a solitary lesion as a simple venous malformation without histology
Underestimating pain as a driver of treatment need
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Surgical excision for localised, symptomatic or painful lesions, which often gives good results
Sclerotherapy or laser as options for lesions less amenable to surgery, recognising the response is less predictable than in common venous malformations
Conservative measures with compression garments and analgesia for symptom relief
Reassurance that lesions are benign and do not undergo malignant change, with monitoring as new lesions may appear over time
Refer to a vascular anomalies multidisciplinary service for treatment planning
Offer molecular confirmation of glomulin (GLMN) variants with genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition and examination of relatives
